concept.name: Cornering the market
concept.definition: Securing such relative control of a commodity or its deliverable supply that its price can be manipulated at the cornerer's will — in the extreme, holding contracts requiring delivery of more of the commodity than is available for delivery. A successful corner forces shorts to cover or settle at prices dictated by the cornerer.
concept.intuition: You quietly buy up nearly everything there is to deliver, so when the sellers must come to market to fulfill their contracts, you're the only shop in town and you name the price.
concept.mechanics: The cornerer accumulates dominant long futures positions approaching delivery while simultaneously controlling the physical deliverable supply. Shorts who cannot find deliverable supply must either buy back futures from the cornerer at inflated prices or pay to acquire the physical commodity from them, producing an artificial price spike.
concept.failure_modes: Corners fail when regulators or exchanges intervene (forced liquidation, limits on price moves), when new deliverable supply appears, or when the cornerer's financing costs overwhelm the squeeze; alleged corners also collapse into ordinary squeezes when the scarcity proves genuine rather than engineered.
concept.misconceptions: A large long position is not itself a corner — dominance plus control of deliverable supply and intent to dictate price are required; likewise, not every short squeeze is a corner, since squeezes can arise naturally from genuine scarcity.
concept.example: The Hunt brothers' 1979-80 accumulation of silver futures and bullion took prices from ~$6 to nearly $50/oz before COMEX rule changes and margin calls broke the corner and prices collapsed.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
